articles.title: Possible meningitis or sepsis in a child: urgent warning awareness
articles.summary: A serious infection may progress rapidly and does not always present with a distinctive rash.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Recognise an evolving illness
paragraphs: Fever, unusual sleepiness, marked irritability, a stiff neck or a new rash may occur in some serious infections, but symptoms vary with age. The absence of one particular sign does not rule out serious illness.

A child who is difficult to wake, has breathing difficulties, a seizure or appears critically unwell needs immediate emergency attention. Do not wait for a rash or use a home checklist to exclude meningitis.

sections.title: Seek urgent professional assessment
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK for immediately life-threatening symptoms. For other concerning changes, obtain urgent clinical advice rather than waiting for all symptoms to appear.
This article is not a diagnosis or treatment guide. Follow the emergency call handler or qualified clinician's advice.

sections.title: Describe the changes
paragraphs: Explain the child's age, what changed from usual behaviour and when the change was first noticed. Mention any uncertainty honestly.
Clinical photographs and symptom-comparison diagrams could falsely reassure and are deferred for qualified review.

articles.title: Asthma-related breathing crisis: recognising a need for urgent help
articles.summary: An asthma-related breathing problem can become serious even when symptoms are not typical.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Recognise changes in breathing
paragraphs: Breathlessness, difficulty speaking normally, unusual effort to breathe or a worsening pattern may be concerning. Not everyone wheezes audibly, and a quiet chest should not be taken as reassurance.
The person's own clinician-provided asthma plan may contain important individual instructions; an offline general article cannot replace it.

sections.title: Escalate without delay
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK if breathing is severely impaired, the person cannot speak normally because of breathlessness, becomes unresponsive or appears in immediate danger. Follow the call handler's instructions.
Do not improvise inhaler doses or substitute somebody else's medicine based on this draft. Treatment instructions require specialist approval.

sections.title: Share useful context
paragraphs: Tell responders what symptoms were observed, any known asthma diagnosis, whether a personal plan is available and what help has already been given.
Device-use and positioning illustrations need qualified review and are not included.

articles.title: Possible carbon monoxide exposure: recognising a hidden household danger
articles.summary: Carbon monoxide cannot be reliably detected by smell, and unexplained illness around combustion appliances needs caution.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Notice a possible exposure pattern
paragraphs: Headache, dizziness, nausea or unusual tiredness may have many causes. Several people feeling unwell in the same building, especially near a fuel-burning appliance, can be an important contextual clue.
A carbon monoxide alarm is a warning device, not a medical test. A silent or absent alarm does not establish that a space is safe.

sections.title: Prioritise safety and emergency help
paragraphs: If carbon monoxide exposure is suspected, move to fresh air without re-entering a potentially hazardous area and seek urgent professional advice. Call 999 in the UK if anyone is seriously unwell or in immediate danger.
Do not attempt appliance diagnosis, gas repairs or repeated entry to gather evidence. Follow emergency services and the relevant gas emergency provider's instructions.

sections.title: Report facts without returning to danger
paragraphs: Share the address, any alarm activation, number of affected people and observed symptoms when speaking with responders, only if known.
Technical airflow or appliance diagrams would require qualified gas-safety review and are deferred.

articles.title: After a water incident: recognising possible breathing complications
articles.summary: Breathing difficulties after submersion need prompt assessment even if the person initially seems better.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Understand why context matters
paragraphs: A person rescued from water may cough, struggle to breathe, become unusually tired or develop other symptoms. The circumstances and symptoms matter more than a simplistic rule about how much water was swallowed.
Do not rely on internet labels such as 'dry drowning' to make a diagnosis. An offline draft cannot determine whether a person is safe.

sections.title: Get appropriate assistance
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK if the person is unresponsive, has serious breathing problems or appears critically unwell. Seek prompt clinical assessment for concerning symptoms after submersion.
Do not put yourself at risk attempting an unsafe rescue. Water rescue and resuscitation procedures are outside this unreviewed draft.

sections.title: Explain the event
paragraphs: If safely known, tell responders where the incident occurred, approximately when and what changes in breathing or responsiveness followed.
Rescue, recovery-position and resuscitation graphics are deferred for expert review.

articles.title: Electrical injury: understanding hidden risks after a shock
articles.summary: An electrical shock can cause harm that is not obvious from the skin's appearance.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Recognise a hazardous scene
paragraphs: An electrical source, damaged cable or wet environment can make the scene dangerous to others. Do not touch a person who may still be in contact with a live source or approach exposed electrical equipment.
An absence of visible burns does not reliably exclude internal injury. Symptoms and exposure circumstances require professional assessment.

sections.title: Seek help without creating another casualty
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK for an immediately dangerous electrical incident, collapse, abnormal breathing or serious injury. Follow emergency service directions and do not attempt electrical repairs.
Only appropriately competent people should isolate or inspect electrical systems. This article provides no switching, testing or rescue technique.

sections.title: Give a factual report
paragraphs: Describe the source and event only from a safe location, noting any observed changes and any help already provided.
Circuit, contact and rescue diagrams are deferred for electrical and medical specialist review.

articles.title: Suspected medicine overdose: when to seek urgent help
articles.summary: Taking too much of a medicine, or the wrong medicine, may be serious even before symptoms appear.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Do not wait for visible symptoms
paragraphs: The medicine, amount, timing and individual circumstances can affect risk. Some harmful effects are delayed, so a person appearing well immediately afterwards is not proof of safety.
Avoid guessing from the package or using a home calculation to decide that an exposure is harmless.

sections.title: Contact appropriate professionals
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK if someone is unconscious, has a seizure, has breathing problems or appears critically unwell. For a suspected overdose without immediate life-threatening symptoms, seek urgent professional advice promptly.
Do not induce vomiting, give additional medication or attempt a home remedy based on this draft. Follow qualified advice.

sections.title: Preserve details safely
paragraphs: If available without delaying help, keep the medicine container or a record of its name and strength to share with clinicians. Be clear about what is known versus estimated.
Dose charts, antidote sequences and treatment diagrams require clinical review and are not provided.

articles.title: Possible heatstroke: recognising severe heat illness
articles.summary: Heat-related illness can become a medical emergency when temperature stress affects awareness or organ function.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Recognise concerning changes
paragraphs: After heat exposure, marked confusion, collapse, seizure or reduced responsiveness can indicate serious illness. Sweating patterns alone do not reliably distinguish mild from severe heat illness.
Consider the setting, activity and person's condition, but do not use an offline article to grade severity.

sections.title: Get emergency help
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK for suspected heatstroke or severe symptoms, and follow the call handler's instructions. Do not delay assistance to complete an observation record.
Cooling treatment methods and specific temperature thresholds require clinically reviewed guidance; none is supplied here.

sections.title: Share useful information
paragraphs: Describe the location, recent heat exposure, activity and observed changes if known. Avoid guessing a core body temperature.
Body-cooling procedures and temperature comparison charts are deferred for specialist review.

articles.title: Anaphylaxis risk: preparing accurate information for responders
articles.summary: A severe allergic reaction may involve breathing, circulation or awareness changes and needs emergency assessment.
articles.needed_for_expert_review: Clinical recognition or treatment illustration requires qualified medical review; no procedural diagram approved.

sections.title: Recognise a serious pattern
paragraphs: Breathing difficulty, throat or tongue swelling, collapse or sudden severe illness after a possible exposure can be concerning. Skin symptoms may be absent, and a previous mild reaction does not predict a future reaction.
A known allergy plan or prescribed emergency device may be relevant, but a general offline draft cannot replace individual training.

sections.title: Escalate promptly
paragraphs: Call 999 in the UK for suspected anaphylaxis and follow emergency instructions. Do not delay the call while looking for a suspected trigger or completing an allergy record.
Adrenaline auto-injector technique, dose and repeat-use instructions require qualified review and are deliberately omitted.

sections.title: Communicate accurately
paragraphs: Share known allergies, suspected exposure, symptom onset and any prescribed treatment already administered, distinguishing facts from guesses.
Anatomical and auto-injector diagrams are marked for expert review rather than embedded.
